newsitem.title: FRANCE: Aziz plays down row with France over Uday.
newsitem.headline: Aziz plays down row with France over Uday.

text.p: An Iraqi minister said on Friday that Baghdad was surprised but not angered by France's decision to refuse medical treatment to President Saddam Hussein's eldest son Uday.

"It was simply a question of him getting better treatment, but his treatment in Iraq will suffice, so it won't be necessary to treat him outside of Iraq," Deputy Prime Minister Tareq Aziz told French television LCI.
Asked if Baghdad held the refusal against France, he replied: "No, we are not putting it in that way."
But he added that Iraq's request for treatment in France for Uday had been humanitarian in nature. "As you know, this was a humanitarian matter. One generally agrees to such a request," he said.

Iraq's ruling Baath party newspaper Thawra said earlier that France would be committing a grave error if it stuck to its decision to refuse treatment to Uday, who was wounded when gunmen opened fire on his car in Baghdad last month.
"If the news is true we will find that the French government would be committing a big mistake if it did so," it said in a front-page editorial.
Uday told a visitor from his hospital bed early this month that four bullets were still lodged in his body.
France announced on Sunday that he would not be allowed treatment on its soil. It gave no reason for the decision, but Thawra said France feared reaction from the United States and Britain.

It called on France to review its policy before "losing many opportunities in the Arab world, most important of them in Iraq." It also lambasted France for its colonial past and what it described as "atrocities" committed against the Arab nation.
During a visit to France this week, Aziz praised Paris for breaking ranks with the United States and Britain in policing a no-fly zone in northern Iraq.
He also urged France to take a more active role in a United Nations commission monitoring Iraq's compliance with U.N. demands for the elimination of its weapons of mass destruction.
He noted that France had the largest share of contracts under Iraq's oil deal with the United Nations allowing Baghdad partial exports worth $2 billion in six months.

But France said the international embargo against Baghdad could be lifted only if Iraq complied with U.N. Security Council resolutions related to the 1991 Gulf war which ousted its troops from Kuwait.
France was Iraq's main Western arms supplier before the war. Baghdad owes Paris more than $5 billion and the French are keen to restore economic ties once the embargo is lifted.
